source_reachability: Statuses I saw myself on 2026-09-16, curl -A Mokaair-editorial. (1) https://openai.com/index/scaling-storage-one-billion-users-part-one/ = HTTP 403, 9,869 bytes, OpenAI edge challenge page carrying <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="360">. NOT a reachable source. Also 403 with near-identical challenge bodies: the no-trailing-slash form (9,866 B), /zh-Hant/index/... (9,915 B), /ja-JP/index/... (9,909 B), /news/engineering/ (9,731 B), /news/engineering/rss.xml (9,773 B), and /careers/software-engineer-habitat-(online-data)-seattle/ (9,912 B). /index/<slug>.json = HTTP 404, 139,753 bytes (genuine origin Next.js 404). (2) https://openai.com/news/rss.xml = HTTP 200, 729,520 bytes, text/xml; live and healthy: 1,196 <item> entries, lastBuildDate 'Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:30:51 GMT', newest item 2026-09-16 16:00:00 GMT; no content:encoded anywhere, so the feed carries metadata only; exactly one item matches this article. (3) https://openai.com/sitemap.xml/engineering/ = HTTP 200, 191,336 bytes, application/xml; 22 <url> entries, of which 20 are articles and two are listing pages (https://openai.com/news/ and https://openai.com/news/engineering/); the part-one entry carries lastmod 2026-09-12T02:19:32.976Z, unchanged from the researcher's fetch; no part-two entry. (4) https://x.com/OpenAIDevs/status/2098502006935814272 = HTTP 200, 197,538 bytes, server-rendered; all three thread posts present verbatim in both visible spans and the embedded full_text fields. (5) https://web.archive.org/web/20260914185323/https://openai.com/index/scaling-storage-one-billion-users-part-one/ = HTTP 200, 552,850 bytes, byte-size identical to the researcher's fetch; /web/20260916235959/... 302s back to it with 'x-archive-redirect-reason: found capture at 20260914185323', so it is the newest capture the Archive holds. This URL is NOT in the researcher's sources[] even though 30 of 37 facts hang off it. web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx = HTTP 503, 11,832 bytes (researcher reported 403 / 24 bytes); archive.org/wayback/available = HTTP 429, matching the researcher. (6) https://openai.com/robots.txt = 200, 98 B; https://openai.com/sitemap.xml = 200, 3,414 B (sitemap index). Net: no first-party route to the article body exists in this container.

refuted.fact: unverified_or_excluded[5]: 'The server-rendered payload exposes no created_at for the tweet; the only timestamp is uploadDate 2026-09-11T20:00:41.000Z on the attached image.'
refuted.why: The x.com payload does expose created_at_ms for every post in the thread: 1789156841000, 1789156844000, 1789156847000 (plus 1789157484000 on a later reply) = 2026-09-11T20:00:41Z, 20:00:44Z and 20:00:47Z UTC. The researcher under-read a page they had in hand and then recorded the gap as a limitation. Material because it fixes the thread at ~10 hours after the 10:00 GMT feed pubDate, which is what stops anyone dating the event from the tweet.

refuted.fact: verified_facts[3]: 'The feed carried 1,194 items with a channel lastBuildDate of Wed, 16 Sep 2026 14:30:47 GMT.'
refuted.why: Two hours later on the same checked_on date I measured 1,196 items and lastBuildDate 'Wed, 16 Sep 2026 16:30:51 GMT'. These are liveness diagnostics of a live document, not facts; recording them as facts guarantees they are wrong by the time anyone reads them. The rest of the fact (pubDate Fri, 11 Sep 2026 10:00:00 GMT, category Engineering, title, link) is confirmed exactly.

It returns HTTP 403 to me on every attempt and in every variant. Nobody checked it on 2026-09-16, and the researcher's own notes say so. Listing an unfetchable page as source[0] while the evidence actually sits on web.archive.org (absent from sources[]) misrepresents the evidence chain and breaks the BRIEF's rule that every fact trace to one url actually fetched.

22 <url> entries, but two are listing pages (https://openai.com/news/ and https://openai.com/news/engineering/). It lists 20 posts. verified_facts[13] gets this right ('lists 22 URLs'); the notes do not, and the notes are what a writer will skim.

refuted.fact: verified_facts[28] quotes, inside quotation marks, 'Each client team is responsible for scaling their own Rockset instance.'
refuted.why: The page reads 'Each client team is responsible for scaling their own Rockset instance for their complex querying needs.' The fact prose truncates inside the quotation marks and supplies a full stop. The verbatim_quote field has the full sentence, so the error is only in the prose a writer would copy from.

refuted.fact: verified_facts[25] quotes 'There are no unbounded queries that can overload Habitat.' as a complete sentence.
refuted.why: The page reads 'There are no unbounded queries that can overload Habitat and complex joins and graph traversals require product teams to do some of the heavy-lifting which helps overall optimize for more efficient designs.' Inserting a full stop mid-sentence turns a qualified clause into a flat absolute about OpenAI's system.

unsupported.fact: sourcing_verdict 'full', and with it verified_facts 0, 1, 2, 5-12 and 15-34 (30 of 37 facts).
unsupported.why: They trace only to web.archive.org, a third-party host, because openai.com/index/* is blocked. The BRIEF is explicit: a fact that exists only behind a blocked page must not be written. I independently re-probed for a first-party route and there is none (locale paths, no-slash form, /news/engineering/, its rss.xml, the .json route and the careers URL all 403; only robots.txt, sitemap.xml, sitemap.xml/<section>/ and news/rss.xml pass, and the feed carries no content:encoded). So the gap is real, not a research failure. The record needs one of two fixes before anyone writes from it: either the editorial lead rules that a verbatim Wayback capture of a first-party page is admissible AND the web.archive.org URL is added to sources[] with its own checked_on, or the piece drops to the researcher's own stated residue (RSS + sitemap + @OpenAIDevs). 'full' is not defensible either way. Note the capture itself checks out as faithful: 552,850 bytes, matching og/twitter meta, and all 23 archive-sourced verbatim quotes match character-for-character.

unsupported.fact: verified_facts[32]: the Figure 01 enumeration listing eight Habitat functions ending '...rate limiting (request shaping), routing, and schema lookup (data residency)'.
unsupported.why: The markup is a strict label|sublabel sequence: Caching|Caches, ACL policies|Authorization, Placement & data residency|Data residency, Encryption|Data security, Isolation|Multi-tenancy, Rate limiting|Request shaping, Routing|'Schema lookup · Data residency'. Read consistently that is seven functions with 'Schema lookup · Data residency' as Routing's sublabel, not eight with routing unlabelled and schema lookup standalone. The researcher's split is one plausible reading presented as fact.

unsupported.fact: verified_facts[14]: the sitemap lastmod is 'the only timestamp OpenAI publishes for this page after the 2026-09-11 publication date'.
unsupported.why: Unverifiable: the page itself is unreachable live and OpenAI publishes on several surfaces (the @OpenAIDevs thread carries 2026-09-11T20:00:41Z, and the page's own 'Keep reading' block prints dates for other posts). The lastmod value 2026-09-12T02:19:32.976Z is confirmed; the word 'only' is not.

It records a forward-looking publication commitment by OpenAI ('In a future post, we'll go into detail about...'). That is a vendor claim and should be flagged true so the copy is forced into 'OpenAI 表示' phrasing; must_not_write[8] already assumes it. Low severity and the opposite of the usual error, but it is the one place a vendor statement is filed as a neutral fact.

additional_findings: MISSED, and it matters for the follow-up framing: immediately after the Rust paragraph the page says 'We plan to share more learnings in a future blog.' That is a SECOND promised follow-up, about the Rust migration, distinct from 'part II' (which is about the storage layer). The researcher recorded the part-II promise twice and never this one, and not_said[9] ('NO DATE FOR PART TWO') does not cover it. Neither has a date.

MISSED: 'Deferring a Python rewrite for a year allowed us to focus on more urgent and impactful challenges during our hypergrowth.' This is the only duration OpenAI gives for the Python-service phase and it is what ties 'by the middle of 2025' to 'In Q2 2026'. A timeline section will want it.

MISSED: the X thread's real timestamps, 2026-09-11T20:00:41Z / 20:00:44Z / 20:00:47Z from created_at_ms in the page the researcher already fetched (see refuted #1). Record them so nobody treats the tweet time as the event time.

MISSED from verified_facts[21]: OpenAI names the cause explicitly - 'Asyncio helps Python execute I/O-bound workloads concurrently, but does not help work around the Python GIL and provide CPU parallelism.' The GIL is the mechanism behind the whole asyncio-jitter section and the fact as written omits it.

BELONGS IN not_said: Figure 03's axis is labelled 'Illustrative time 0.0 / 40 illustrative units' and its caption is explicitly illustrative. OpenAI therefore publishes NO measured latency chart at all - the only latency figures anywhere on the page are the 'hundreds of milliseconds ... in some edge cases several seconds' jitter range and the unquantified 'significantly lower average and tail latencies'.

CONTEXT that supports the researcher's (correct) date handling: the page's own 'Keep reading' block dates three other Engineering posts Aug 25 2026, Aug 3 2026 and Jul 29 2026, while the engineering sitemap gives those same URLs lastmod values of 2026-09-15 and 2026-09-16. That is direct proof inside these very sources that sitemap lastmod is a build timestamp, not a publication date - useful if anyone later questions why 2026-09-12 was not used as the event date.

VERIFIED NOT GUESSED, so do not re-litigate: the three outbound links in verified_facts[23], [25] and [34] all appear as real hrefs in the capture - https://engineering.fb.com/2014/11/14/production-engineering/solving-the-mystery-of-link-imbalance-a-metastable-failure-state-at-scale/ (metastable failure), https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/atc13/atc13-bronson.pdf (TAO), and https://openai.com/careers/software-engineer-habitat-(online-data)-seattle/ (the job advert, which itself 403s here and so may be described but not cited as a source).

VERIFIED by my own string counts against the capture: '22M' appears 0 times in body text and only in meta tags/JSON (9 raw-HTML hits); '22 million' 0 times; 'durability', 'backup', 'replica', 'SLA', 'uptime', 'restore' and 'disaster recovery' 0 times each; 'Nanobase' once, inside the diagram only. The 'GPT-5.5' in the Rust sentence is confirmed U+2011 (codepoint 0x2011), unlike the ordinary hyphen in the site footer's 'GPT-5.5' nav link - so that sentence must be copied, not retyped. The og:image:alt and twitter:image:alt on the OpenAI page itself both say 'nearly 1 billion' while og:title says 'over 1 billion', confirming verified_facts[36] from the article page and not only from the X card.

NO DISQUALIFYING SOURCE: nothing is traced to a news outlet, aggregator, law-firm blog or search snippet; the excluded list (HackerNoon, daily.dev, dotnetramblings, braindetox.kr, aiposthub, YouTube, fxtwitter) is handled correctly. NO DATE CONFLATION: 2026-09-11 (feed pubDate plus the page-printed date), 2026-09-12 (sitemap build), 2026-09-14 (capture) and the X thread time are kept properly apart, and event_date 2026-09-11 is right. These are the two things that usually go wrong and the researcher got both right.

The feed's <link> is https://openai.com/index/scaling-storage-one-billion-users-part-one with NO trailing slash, while sources[0] has one. Both 403, so it changes nothing, but if the content pack cites the canonical URL it should match the feed's spelling.
